coordination_note: Canonical deep-build of § 1030 for financial fraud RICO predicates lives in US_Federal_Financial_Fraud_Litigator. This standard is built from the telecom/unauthorized-access angle: SIM swap attacks, device takeover, digital surveillance, and Ryan McClaran IT operator conduct. Both builds are independently justified by domain scope differences.
cases_to_add: hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn (9th Cir. 2022) — 'without authorization' requires affirmative revocation; public access cannot be 'unauthorized'
United States v. Nosal (9th Cir. 2012 / 2016) — exceeds authorized access requires gates/barriers, not mere policy violation; SIM swap analogy
steward_relevance: Post-SIM-swap, attackers had access to phone-based authentication across email, financial, and government accounts. Each unauthorized login after a SIM swap is a separate § 1030(a)(2)(C) violation (unauthorized access to protected computer + obtains information). § 1030(g) civil private right of action requires showing: loss exceeding $5,000 in a 1-year period OR impairment of medical examination. AT&T carrier conduct enabling the SIM swap may also constitute § 1030(a)(2) aiding.
first_step_triage: Post-SIM-swap: identify each account that was accessed (email, financial, phone), when (timestamp from carrier logs), and what information was obtained. Each unauthorized session is a discrete § 1030 violation. Damages calculation under § 1030(c)(4)(A)(i)(I) = investigative and remediation costs + imputed value of data accessed. Civil filing threshold: $5,000 aggregate loss within one-year period.
